sources.0.title: Artemis II: Crewed Lunar Flyby (checked 2026-09-26)
intro: Artemis lunar crews will observe, describe, and collect samples as geologists. Classroom petrology and field training in New Mexico and Iceland prepare them to interpret permanently shadowed regions and water ice at the South Pole.
lessons.0.title: Why Astronauts Study Geology
lessons.0.summary: Lunar stays are short. If the crew cannot read the rocks on-site, the stones brought back to Earth will remain merely 'clean rocks,' missing the scientific objectives.
lessons.0.body.0: Official NASA training reports state that geology is a core subject in the curriculum, citing the possibility that candidates may be assigned to future Artemis lunar missions. The 2025 class completed classroom instruction at Johnson Space Center, followed by fieldwork at Rio Grande del Norte National Monument in New Mexico in May 2026, where they practiced observation, sampling, navigation, and teamwork.
lessons.0.body.1: Since Apollo, lunar scientific results have depended on the crew's eyes. Remote researchers cannot see the on-site light, shadows, and layer continuity. The crew's ability to document 'what they see and why they collect it' in a single sentence determines the value of the samples.
lessons.0.body.2: In July, some candidates joined NASA astronauts, the Artemis support team, and geology instructors for field training in Iceland. JAXA astronaut Takuya Onishi was officially recorded as participating as well. This serves as practice in using a common observational language across different national operational cultures.
lessons.0.facts.0.label: Classroom
lessons.0.facts.1.label: Field Example
lessons.0.deepDive.title: Connecting Observation, Interpretation, and Sample Provenance
lessons.0.deepDive.body.0: Rock color and grain size are observations; the processes that formed them are interpretations. Recording the location and surrounding terrain before collection allows for later evaluation of hypotheses regarding whether a fragment was transported from elsewhere or represents the local stratigraphy.
lessons.0.deepDive.body.1: The rocks and survey sites in this game are fictional configurations. While the terrain is modeled using NASA elevation data to practice observation procedures, it does not guarantee the composition of specific locations. One cannot definitively conclude the presence of water ice based solely on dark areas in images. Distinguish between what is known from observation and what requires additional measurement.
lessons.1.title: Bright Highlands and Dark Seas: The Moon's Dichotomy
lessons.1.summary: The bright feldspar-rich highlands and the dark basaltic seas differ in both formation era and composition. Sampling plans begin with this map.
lessons.1.body.0: NASA's lunar science explanations broadly divide the lunar surface into bright highlands and dark maria. The highlands consist of feldspar-rich anorthosite, recorded as the result of light minerals floating and solidifying from the early magma ocean. The maria are areas where later basaltic lava filled basins; they are rich in iron and titanium and have low reflectivity.
lessons.1.body.1: Samples returned by Apollo turned this dichotomy into laboratory numbers. However, landing sites were biased toward low-latitude, near-side locations. The South Pole region features adjacent highland material, ejecta from giant impacts, and volatile components in permanently shadowed areas. Even for the same 'rock,' misidentifying the unit it stands on can cause interpretations to collapse from the foundation.
lessons.1.body.2: In the field, first observe color, grain size, fracture patterns, and the arrangement of surrounding boulders. Before breaking with a hammer, distinguish between upper and lower stratigraphic layers, and between weathered and fresh surfaces. Since the Moon has no atmosphere, erosion like Earth's rivers or forests does not occur. Instead, micrometeorites and solar radiation break down the surface layer to create regolith.
lessons.1.facts.0.label: Highlands
lessons.1.facts.1.label: Maria
lessons.2.title: The South Pole: Light and Shadow as Scientific Objectives
lessons.2.summary: Low solar elevation creates long shadows, potentially trapping volatile components in depressions that never receive sunlight.
lessons.2.body.0: As confirmed by NASA plans on September 26, 2026, Artemis III is a mission to demonstrate systems necessary for future lunar landings in low Earth orbit, with landing operations positioned for Artemis IV and beyond. The importance of South Pole science and training should be understood separately from mission numbering. At the South Pole, the sun circles near the horizon; high rims receive prolonged sunlight, while depression bottoms can become permanently shadowed regions (PSRs). The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has continuously mapped this terrain, temperature, and illumination.
lessons.2.body.1: Sunlit ridges are suitable for power generation and communication, while adjacent shadows are candidate sites for water ice. In a walking EVA, temperature and appearance change within a few steps from bright to dark areas. Before crossing the edge of a shadow, assess the next foothold, time, and power.
lessons.2.body.2: From Earth, the South Pole is often hidden at the limb. Before landing, crews must internalize 'which rim blocks the sun' using LRO oblique lighting images and digital elevation models. On-site, the direction of one's own shadow serves as a clock.
lessons.2.facts.0.label: Plan Confirmation
lessons.2.facts.1.label: Map
lessons.3.title: Craters are both clocks and libraries
lessons.3.summary: New impacts excavate older strata and deposit ejecta. Learn to distinguish rims, floors, central peaks, and secondary craters.
lessons.3.body.0: The age of the lunar surface is read not only through radiometric dating but also through crater density and superposition relationships. Newer craters cut into older ground, and their ejecta blankets the surroundings. The vertical order of these overlaps provides the first clue to relative dating.
lessons.3.body.1: Ejecta from large basins places 'foreign rock' on distant highlands. Samples from the polar regions mix locally formed rock with material thrown in from far away. Samples that do not note in the collection log whether they are local bedrock, erratics, or ejecta will cause problems for the laboratory later.
lessons.3.body.2: In field training, instructors repeatedly ask, 'Is the surface you are looking at primary or secondary?' Lava and erosion landscapes in Iceland or New Mexico are not the Moon itself. Nevertheless, the actions of pointing to layers, pacing out distances, and drawing the same sketches as a team can be transferred to short EVAs on the lunar surface.
lessons.3.facts.0.label: Relative Dating
lessons.3.facts.1.label: Caution
lessons.3.facts.1.value: Mixing of Ejecta and Local Bedrock
lessons.4.title: Water ice is not just 'present' but 'where and in what state'
lessons.4.summary: The low temperatures of permanently shadowed regions can retain volatile components. Collection procedures must account for contamination and sublimation.
lessons.4.body.0: NASA's lunar science treats the possibility that volatile components, such as water ice, are retained in the permanently shadowed regions of the poles, based on spacecraft observations. The ice may be surface frost or grains mixed into the regolith. Depth, concentration, and location all vary.
lessons.4.body.1: In places where sunlight does not reach, camera dynamic range and human adaptation cannot keep up. Change the angle of the headlamp, verbalize observations, and check temperature and time before collection. Do not put samples that are lost the moment they are warmed into the same bags as Earth rocks.
lessons.4.body.2: The science goals of Artemis include both water as a resource and the record of early solar system volatiles. Crews must not confuse 'usable ice' with 'ice that preserves age information.' Which to collect is determined by that day's flight plan and the priorities of the ground science team.
lessons.4.facts.0.label: Retention Conditions
lessons.4.facts.1.label: Hazard
lessons.5.title: Observation begins before the hammer
lessons.5.summary: Describe color, grain size, structure, and contact relationships in words before opening the sample bag. Photos are the evidence for those words.
lessons.5.body.0: Official field training includes not only the handling of collection tools but also geological observation itself as a subject. Candidates who have examined rock thin sections and hand samples in the classroom use the same vocabulary in the field. Plagioclase cleavage, basalt vesicles, clast matrix and fragments. List the visible properties before naming them.
lessons.5.body.1: On the Moon, time is short. Therefore, on Earth, we repeat the exercise: 'State three features in 30 seconds.' Fix position with maps and photos, and fix orientation with the Sun and known ridges. Match sample numbers and photo numbers on the spot.
lessons.5.body.2: Preparation articles for Artemis II also list science preparation and geological training as independent pillars. Even for flyby missions, training to 'see' the Moon passes observational language to future landing crews.
lessons.5.facts.0.label: Record First
lessons.5.facts.1.label: Record Later
lessons.6.title: Sampling is a procedure toward science goals
lessons.6.summary: The value is determined not by the number of rocks collected, but by whether the context is preserved. Make the bag, tag, photo, and verbal report into one sample.
lessons.6.body.0: Field training explicitly includes collection using tools. Scoops, tongs, hammers, cores. Which to use depends on whether the target is a rock fragment or fine grain, or if it is a volatile component that is sensitive to contamination. Oil from gloves and dust from Earth also become part of the sample.
lessons.6.body.1: The skeleton of the procedure is simple. Wide shot, medium shot, close-up. A scale indicating orientation. Collection. Additional photos if there are cross-sections or fracture openings. Close the bag, read out the number, and record ground disturbance before walking to the next location. On the Moon, footprints themselves are geological alteration.
lessons.6.body.2: The ground science team updates the next priorities based on the crew's verbal reports and images. Communication delay is small, but EVA time is short. Therefore, practice on the slopes of Iceland the judgment of 'should we collect now, or can it wait?' based on the target list and remaining time.
lessons.6.facts.0.label: Essential
lessons.6.facts.1.label: Prohibited
lessons.7.title: Earth is a compass and an anchor for the mind
lessons.7.summary: Earth floating in the polar sky serves as a reference for orientation, communication, and confirming where you are standing.
lessons.7.body.0: At the lunar south pole, there are times when Earth appears large near the horizon. Earthshine slightly aids work in shadows, while the orientation of the 'blue disc' provides a rough directional cue. Precise navigation relies on inertial systems, maps, and beacons, but human situational awareness is stabilized by the view of Earth in the sky.
lessons.7.body.1: Official lunar science positions the Moon as a neighbor that preserves Earth's history. This includes its environment near the magnetosphere's edge, records of giant impacts, and volatile components. The act of crew looking up at Earth is not merely sentimental; it is a reminder of 'which planetary system' the samples belong to.
lessons.7.body.2: Communication depends on line-of-sight to Earth and relay satellites. If you enter the shadow of a ridge, voice contact is lost. Even if geological targets are attractive, do not venture into areas where links, power, and return paths are not visible. Navigation is a safety subject equal in importance to geology.
lessons.7.facts.0.label: Cue
lessons.7.facts.1.label: Constraint
lessons.7.facts.1.value: Line of sight and ridge shadows
lessons.8.title: Orion and the Lander: Transport Constraints Shape Science
lessons.8.summary: Sampling time is determined by spacecraft design. Geological plans must fit within the margins of life support, power, and ascent reserves.
lessons.8.body.0: In Artemis, transport systems such as SLS, Orion, and the crewed lander support scientific activities. Since mission configurations and schedules change, distinguish between historical training articles and current mission pages. Johnson's Mission Control officially states that it supervises not only the ISS but also the round-trip Artemis lunar flights. Crew geological activities are embedded in this transport system's timeline.
lessons.8.body.1: According to NASA's mission page, Artemis II is a crewed lunar flyby launched on April 1, 2026, and returned on April 10. Distinguish this from flights that stay in lunar orbit. Geological training articles from the preparation phase indicate that even flights without a landing required practice in observing lunar surface features.
lessons.8.body.2: The number of EVAs and walking radius are limited by spacesuit wear, dust, heat, and life support reserves. Even if the desired rock is on the other side of a hill, do not move the return time. This is why field training requires experiencing the decision to 'abandon a target' in advance.
lessons.8.facts.0.label: Lunar Flyby
lessons.8.facts.1.label: III Plan
lessons.8.facts.1.value: Crewed demonstration in Low Earth Orbit
lessons.9.title: Translating Earth Fieldwork to Lunar Procedures
lessons.9.summary: Canyons in New Mexico or lava fields in Iceland are not the Moon. What is translated is not the terrain, but the pattern of observation.
lessons.9.body.0: At Rio Grande del Norte, candidates gather for group photos holding rock samples and point at features while walking over hills. Official descriptions state that observation, tool-assisted sampling, navigation, and teamwork translate directly to Artemis lunar surface missions.
lessons.9.body.1: The translation is specific: ignore Earth's vegetation and clouds, looking only at layers, contacts, and talus. Use the clock and remaining water to determine the next outcrop. Use radio to convey 'what is visible now and what to collect next' to the ground team. On the lunar surface, the counterpart becomes the Houston science officer.
lessons.9.body.2: The course is approximately two years long, with the 2025 class expected to graduate in 2027. The first flight after graduation may be to the ISS. Nevertheless, the geological pattern is not discarded. The observation skills used in short lunar EVAs are the same 'muscles' used in routine maintenance inspections.
lessons.9.facts.0.label: Translation Target
lessons.9.facts.1.label: Graduation
quiz.0.prompt: Which location is officially recorded as the site of the field geological training conducted by the 2025 class in May 2026?
quiz.0.explanation: The official summer report states that after classroom instruction at Johnson, field training was conducted at Rio Grande del Norte in New Mexico.
quiz.1.prompt: In the same official report, which JAXA astronaut is specifically named as accompanying the July Iceland field training?
quiz.1.explanation: The article records that Akihiko Hoshide, along with candidates Cameron Jones and Yuri Kubo, participated in the geological field training in Iceland.
quiz.2.prompt: Which rock is said to primarily constitute the bright highlands of the Moon?
quiz.2.explanation: NASA's lunar science describes the bright highlands as anorthosite rich in plagioclase. The dark maria are basaltic lava.
quiz.3.prompt: Which rock primarily fills the dark 'maria' of the Moon?
quiz.3.explanation: Mare are regions where later basaltic lava filled basins; they are rich in iron and titanium and have low reflectivity.
quiz.4.prompt: According to NASA plans confirmed on September 26, 2026, which vehicle demonstrates lunar landing systems in low Earth orbit?
quiz.4.explanation: Current NASA pages describe Artemis III as a crewed demonstration in low Earth orbit. This is distinct from past plans that described 'Artemis III' as a lunar landing.
quiz.5.prompt: Which NASA orbiter has continuously mapped the topography, temperature, and illumination of the lunar poles?
quiz.5.explanation: LRO observes the lunar surface in high resolution, supporting the understanding of permanent shadows and illumination conditions at the south pole.
quiz.6.prompt: What is the primary clue for distinguishing new rock layers from old ones on the lunar surface in the field?
quiz.6.choices.0: Brightness as seen from Earth only
quiz.6.choices.2: Overlapping and cutting of craters and ejecta
quiz.6.explanation: Newer impacts cut older ground, and ejecta covers the surroundings. Overlap relationships are the basis of relative dating.
quiz.7.prompt: Which is the appropriate reason why water ice is likely to be preserved in polar regions?
quiz.7.choices.0: The entire lunar surface is always 0°C
quiz.7.choices.3: The low temperatures in permanent shadows make it difficult for volatile components to escape
quiz.7.explanation: The low temperatures in permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) can preserve volatile components such as water ice; this is a basic framework of NASA lunar science.
quiz.8.prompt: What does official candidate geological training list as a subject alongside tool handling?
quiz.8.explanation: Summer reports list observation, collection, navigation, and teamwork, stating that these translate to lunar surface missions.
quiz.9.prompt: What most determines the scientific value of lunar samples?
quiz.9.choices.1: Context such as collection location, photos, and oral descriptions
quiz.9.choices.2: The visual beauty of the rocks
quiz.9.choices.3: Shapes commonly seen in Earth museums
quiz.9.explanation: Samples without context cannot be interpreted in the laboratory. Photos, numbers, locations, and oral descriptions are part of the sample.
quiz.10.prompt: What significance of seeing Earth in the sky at the lunar south pole does this lesson emphasize?
quiz.10.choices.0: Seeing Earth causes permanent shadows to disappear
quiz.10.choices.1: The color of Earth determines rock types
quiz.10.choices.2: It provides clues for orientation, situational awareness, and communication line-of-sight
quiz.10.choices.3: Earthshine alone allows for precision landing
quiz.10.explanation: Earth serves as a rough orientation and psychological anchor, while also prompting awareness of communication line-of-sight directions. It is not a substitute for precision navigation.
quiz.11.prompt: Which mission conducted a crewed lunar flyby with Orion in April 2026?
quiz.11.explanation: NASA records Artemis II as a crewed lunar flyby. It launched on April 1, 2026, and returned on April 10. This is distinct from lunar landing or insertion into lunar orbit.
quiz.12.prompt: Which is the correct description of permanently shadowed regions (PSRs)?
quiz.12.choices.0: Areas where the solar elevation is low and sunlight barely reaches the bottom of depressions
quiz.12.choices.1: The phenomenon where Earth's shadow covers the entire Moon
quiz.12.choices.2: Another name for the far side where Earth is always invisible
quiz.12.choices.3: A general term for highlands where stars are visible even during the day
quiz.12.explanation: At the south pole, the low sun is blocked by rims, allowing depressions to remain in shadow for extremely long periods. These are candidates for preserving volatile components.
quiz.13.prompt: Which skills does an official article state are 'directly translated' from Earth field training to the lunar surface?
quiz.13.choices.1: Geological observation, collection, navigation, and teamwork
quiz.13.explanation: Training in Rio Grande del Norte and Iceland is designed to transfer observation, tool-assisted collection, navigation, and teamwork to lunar surface procedures.
quiz.14.prompt: What does Johnson's Mission Control officially state it will oversee, in addition to the ISS?
quiz.14.choices.0: Only the day shift of Mars uncrewed rovers
quiz.14.choices.2: Artemis flights including lunar round trips
quiz.14.choices.3: Plans prior to the assembly of the International Space Station only
quiz.14.explanation: The official description of the Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center states that, in addition to 24-hour monitoring of the ISS, it oversees Artemis lunar round trips.
quiz.15.prompt: For samples from permanently shadowed regions that may contain volatile components, what should be particularly avoided?
quiz.15.choices.2: Oral reporting to the ground science team
quiz.15.choices.3: Heating them and placing them in the same bag as ordinary rocks
quiz.15.explanation: Samples that sublime or alter due to heat and contamination require temperature management and a clean collection system, separate from context recording.
glossary.0.description: Bright rock rich in plagioclase. It represents the lunar highlands and is considered a record of the differentiation of the early magma ocean.
glossary.1.description: Regions where dark basaltic lava filled basins. Rich in iron and titanium, and younger than the highlands.
glossary.2.description: The unconsolidated surface layer crushed by micrometeorite impacts and other processes. It is the medium for lunar walking and sample collection, and it wears down machinery and spacesuits.
glossary.3.description: Regions such as polar depressions that receive little to no sunlight, maintaining low temperatures capable of preserving volatile components like water ice.
glossary.4.description: Material excavated and scattered by impacts. It mixes with the local substrate, complicating the interpretation of sample origins.
glossary.5.description: A NASA orbiter that maps the Moon at high resolution, providing foundational data for terrain, temperature, illumination, and landing site assessment.
glossary.6.description: A crewed mission, confirmed in a September 2026 plan, to demonstrate systems required for future lunar landings in low Earth orbit.
glossary.7.description: A deep-space crewed spacecraft. It is tasked with transporting crews to and from the Moon in Artemis, with a crewed orbital flight planned for the second unit.
glossary.8.description: A station planned as a crewed outpost in lunar proximity, serving as a hub for transportation, science, and habitation.
glossary.9.description: The phenomenon where light reflected from Earth faintly illuminates the Moon's night side. It can assist with operations and orientation in the shadows of the south pole.
